  10 │ >>> def print_attrs(cls):
  11 │ ...     print(cls.__attrs_attrs__)
  12 │ ...     return cls
  13 │ >>> @print_attrs
  14 │ ... @define
  15 │ ... class C:
  16 │ ...     a: int
  17 │ (Attribute(name='a', default=NOTHING, validator=None, repr=True, eq=True, eq_key=None, order=True, order_key=None, hash=None, init=True, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=<class 'int'>, converter=None, kw_only=False, inherited=False, on_setattr=None, alias='a'),)

  21 │ The {func}`attrs.define` / {func}`attr.s` decorator **must** be applied first because it puts `__attrs_attrs__` in place!
  22 │ That means that is has to come *after* your decorator because:
  23 │ 
  24 │ ```python

  26 │ @b
  27 │ def f():
  28 │    pass
  29 │ ```
  30 │ 
  31 │ is just [syntactic sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syntactic_sugar) for:
  32 │ 
  33 │ ```python

  35 │    pass
  36 │ 
  37 │ f = a(b(original_f))
  38 │ ```

  40 │ 
  41 │ 
  42 │ ## Wrapping the Decorator
  43 │ 
  44 │ A more elegant way can be to wrap *attrs* altogether and build a class [DSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-specific_language) on top of it.

  46 │ An example for that is the package [*environ-config*](https://github.com/hynek/environ-config) that uses *attrs* under the hood to define environment-based configurations declaratively without exposing *attrs* APIs at all.

  62 │ )
  63 │

  65 │ attr_dataclass_makers.add("my_module.method_looks_like_attr_dataclass")

  68 │ attr_class_makers.add("my_module.method_looks_like_attr_s")
  69 │ 
  70 │ # These are our `attr.ib` makers.
  71 │ attr_attrib_makers.add("my_module.method_looks_like_attrib")
  72 │ 
  73 │ class MyPlugin(Plugin):
  74 │     # Our plugin does nothing but it has to exist so this file gets loaded.
  75 │     pass
  76 │ 
  77 │ 
  78 │ def plugin(version):

 107 │ ## Types
 108 │ 
 109 │ *attrs* offers two ways of attaching type information to attributes:
 110 │ 
 111 │ - {pep}`526` annotations,
 112 │ - and the *type* argument to {func}`attr.ib` / {func}`attrs.field`.

 115 │ 
 116 │ ```{doctest}
 117 │ >>> from attrs import define, field, fields
 118 │ >>> @define
 119 │ ... class C:
 120 │ ...     x: int = field()
 121 │ ...     y = field(type=str)

 124 │ >>> fields(C).y.type

 136 │ ## Metadata
 137 │ 
 138 │ If you're the author of a third-party library with *attrs* integration, you may want to take advantage of attribute metadata.
 139 │ 
 140 │ Here are some tips for effective use of metadata:
 141 │ 
 142 │ - Try making your metadata keys and values immutable.
 143 │   This keeps the entire {class}`~attrs.Attribute` instances immutable too.
 144 │ 
 145 │ - To avoid metadata key collisions, consider exposing your metadata keys from your modules.:
 146 │ 
 147 │   ```python
 148 │   from mylib import MY_METADATA_KEY
 149 │ 
 150 │   @define
 151 │   class C:
 152 │     x = field(metadata={MY_METADATA_KEY: 1})
 153 │   ```
 154 │ 
 155 │   Metadata should be composable, so consider supporting this approach even if you decide implementing your metadata in one of the following ways.
 156 │ 
 157 │ - Expose `field` wrappers for your specific metadata.
 158 │   This is a more graceful approach if your users don't require metadata from other libraries.
 159 │ 
 160 │   ```{doctest}
 161 │   >>> from attrs import fields, NOTHING
 162 │   >>> MY_TYPE_METADATA = '__my_type_metadata'
 163 │   >>>
 164 │   >>> def typed(
 165 │   ...     cls, default=NOTHING, validator=None, repr=True,
 166 │   ...     eq=True, order=None, hash=None, init=True, metadata=None,
 167 │   ...     converter=None
 168 │   ... ):
 169 │   ...     metadata = metadata or {}
 170 │   ...     metadata[MY_TYPE_METADATA] = cls
 171 │   ...     return field(
 172 │   ...         default=default, validator=validator, repr=repr,
 173 │   ...         eq=eq, order=order, hash=hash, init=init,
 174 │   ...         metadata=metadata, converter=converter
 175 │   ...     )
 176 │   >>>
 177 │   >>> @define
 178 │   ... class C:
 179 │   ...     x: int = typed(int, default=1, init=False)
 180 │   >>> fields(C).x.metadata[MY_TYPE_METADATA]
 181 │   <class 'int'>
 182 │   ```

 184 │ (transform-fields)=

 186 │ ## Automatic Field Transformation and Modification
 187 │ 
 188 │ *attrs* allows you to automatically modify or transform the class' fields while the class is being created.
 189 │ You do this by passing a *field_transformer* hook to {func}`~attrs.define` (and friends).
 190 │ Its main purpose is to automatically add converters to attributes based on their type to aid the development of API clients and other typed data loaders.
 191 │ 
 192 │ This hook must have the following signature:
 193 │ 
 194 │ ```{eval-rst}
 195 │ .. function:: your_hook(cls: type, fields: list[attrs.Attribute]) -> list[attrs.Attribute]
 196 │    :noindex:
 197 │ ```
 198 │ 
 199 │ - *cls* is your class right *before* it is being converted into an attrs class.
 200 │   This means it does not yet have the `__attrs_attrs__` attribute.
 201 │ - *fields* is a list of all `attrs.Attribute` instances that will later be set to `__attrs_attrs__`.
 202 │   You can modify these attributes any way you want:
 203 │   You can add converters, change types, and even remove attributes completely or create new ones!
 204 │ 
 205 │ For example, let's assume that you really don't like floats:
 206 │ 
 207 │ ```{doctest}
 208 │ >>> def drop_floats(cls, fields):
 209 │ ...     return [f for f in fields if f.type not in {float, 'float'}]
 210 │ ...
 211 │ >>> @frozen(field_transformer=drop_floats)
 212 │ ... class Data:
 213 │ ...     a: int
 214 │ ...     b: float
 215 │ ...     c: str
 216 │ ...
 217 │ >>> Data(42, "spam")
 218 │ Data(a=42, c='spam')
 219 │ ```
 220 │ 
 221 │ A more realistic example would be to automatically convert data that you, for example, load from JSON:
 222 │ 
 223 │ ```{doctest}
 224 │ >>> from datetime import datetime
 225 │ >>>
 226 │ >>> def auto_convert(cls, fields):
 227 │ ...     results = []
 228 │ ...     for field in fields:
 229 │ ...         if field.converter is not None:
 230 │ ...             results.append(field)
 231 │ ...             continue
 232 │ ...         if field.type in {datetime, 'datetime'}:
 233 │ ...             converter = (lambda d: datetime.fromisoformat(d) if isinstance(d, str) else d)
 234 │ ...         else:
 235 │ ...             converter = None
 236 │ ...         results.append(field.evolve(converter=converter))
 237 │ ...     return results
 238 │ ...
 239 │ >>> @frozen(field_transformer=auto_convert)
 240 │ ... class Data:
 241 │ ...     a: int
 242 │ ...     b: str
 243 │ ...     c: datetime
 244 │ ...
 245 │ >>> from_json = {"a": 3, "b": "spam", "c": "2020-05-04T13:37:00"}
 246 │ >>> Data(**from_json)  # ****
 247 │ Data(a=3, b='spam', c=datetime.datetime(2020, 5, 4, 13, 37))
 248 │ ```
 249 │ 
 250 │ Or, perhaps you would prefer to generate dataclass-compatible `__init__` signatures via a default field *alias*.
 251 │ Note, *field_transformer* receives {class}`attrs.Attribute` instances with default aliases already resolved, so the leading-underscore stripping has already been applied.
 252 │ You can use the `attrs.Attribute.alias_is_default` flag to detect whether an alias was explicitly provided by the user or auto-generated.
 253 │ 
 254 │ ```{doctest}
 255 │ >>> def dataclass_names(cls, fields):
 256 │ ...     return [
 257 │ ...         field.evolve(alias=field.name)
 258 │ ...         if field.alias_is_default
 259 │ ...         else field
 260 │ ...         for field in fields
 261 │ ...     ]
 262 │ ...
 263 │ >>> @frozen(field_transformer=dataclass_names)
 264 │ ... class Data:
 265 │ ...     public: int
 266 │ ...     _private: str
 267 │ ...     explicit: str = field(alias="aliased_name")
 268 │ ...
 269 │ >>> Data(public=42, _private="spam", aliased_name="yes")
 270 │ Data(public=42, _private='spam', explicit='yes')
 271 │ ```
 272 │ 
 273 │ ## Customize Value Serialization in `asdict()`
 274 │ 
 275 │ *attrs* allows you to serialize instances of *attrs* classes to dicts using the {func}`attrs.asdict` function.
 276 │ However, the result can not always be serialized since most data types will remain as they are:
 277 │ 
 278 │ ```{doctest}
 279 │ >>> import json
 280 │ >>> import datetime
 281 │ >>> from attrs import asdict
 282 │ >>>
 283 │ >>> @frozen
 284 │ ... class Data:
 285 │ ...    dt: datetime.datetime
 286 │ ...
 287 │ >>> data = asdict(Data(datetime.datetime(2020, 5, 4, 13, 37)))
 288 │ >>> data
 289 │ {'dt': datetime.datetime(2020, 5, 4, 13, 37)}
 290 │ >>> json.dumps(data)
 291 │ Traceback (most recent call last):
 292 │    ...
 293 │ TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable
 294 │ ```
 295 │ 
 296 │ To help you with this, {func}`~attrs.asdict` allows you to pass a *value_serializer* hook.
 297 │ It has the signature
 298 │ 
 299 │ ```{eval-rst}
 300 │ .. function:: your_hook(inst: type, field: attrs.Attribute, value: typing.Any) -> typing.Any
 301 │    :noindex:
 302 │ ```
 303 │ 
 304 │ ```{doctest}
 305 │ >>> from attr import asdict
 306 │ >>> def serialize(inst, field, value):
 307 │ ...     if isinstance(value, datetime.datetime):
 308 │ ...         return value.isoformat()
 309 │ ...     return value
 310 │ ...
 311 │ >>> data = asdict(
 312 │ ...     Data(datetime.datetime(2020, 5, 4, 13, 37)),
 313 │ ...     value_serializer=serialize,
 314 │ ... )
 315 │ >>> data
 316 │ {'dt': '2020-05-04T13:37:00'}
 317 │ >>> json.dumps(data)
 318 │ '{"dt": "2020-05-04T13:37:00"}'
 319 │ ```

## Plan

**What the reference adds (the target version)**

The reference directory `/megabit/.megabit_ref` contains a new file, `changelog.d/1509.breaking.md`. It says two things: field aliases are now worked out *before* the field transformer runs, so the transformer sees each field with a real alias value instead of an empty one; and there is a new flag on each field, `alias_is_default`, which is `True` when the alias was made up automatically and `False` when the person set it themselves.

**Files that differ**

- `/workspace/src/attr/_make.py` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/src/attr/_make.py`
- `/workspace/docs/extending.md` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/docs/extending.md`
- `/workspace/tests/test_functional.py`, `/workspace/tests/test_hooks.py`, `/workspace/tests/test_make.py`, `/workspace/tests/utils.py` (each has a reference counterpart that differs)
- `/workspace/CHANGELOG.md` and `/workspace/.git_archival.txt` differ from the reference; `uv.lock` exists only in the workspace.

**What I actually read**

I read `/workspace/docs/extending.md` and `/megabit/.megabit_ref/docs/extending.md` in full. Both describe the field transformer hook. The workspace version (around line 250-251) says the transformer runs "before the default private-attribute handling is applied so explicit user-provided aliases can be detected," and its example checks `if not field.alias`. The reference version (line 250-252) instead says the transformer "receives Attribute instances with default aliases already resolved, so the leading-underscore stripping has already been applied," and its example checks the new `field.alias_is_default` flag instead of `not field.alias`.

I also read `/megabit/.megabit_ref/changelog.d/1509.breaking.md` in full.

I searched `/workspace/src/attr/_make.py` and `/megabit/.megabit_ref/src/attr/_make.py` for alias and transformer handling. In the workspace, the transformer is called first (around line 466) and the default alias is filled in afterwards (around lines 483-489). In the reference, the default alias is filled in first (around lines 466-473, setting `alias_is_default` to `True`), then the transformer runs, and any fields the transformer adds get their alias filled afterwards too. The reference also adds `alias_is_default` to the field's stored values, its printed form, its comparison/evolve handling, and its saved/loaded state.

**What is missing or wrong for the user today**

Today, when someone writes a field transformer, the fields they receive do not yet have their automatic alias filled in — the alias value is empty for fields the person did not name explicitly. So a transformer cannot tell "this field got its name automatically" apart from "this field has no alias yet," and it has to guess using the empty value. The reference fixes both: aliases are ready before the transformer runs, and there is a clear flag for automatic vs. hand-set aliases.

{"file_path":"/megabit/ticket.md","content":"# My field helper cannot tell an automatic name from one I picked myself

## What happens now

When I write a helper that looks at each field of my class, the fields I get do not yet have their automatic names filled in. The name slot is empty for any field whose name I did not set by hand. Because the slot is empty, I cannot tell a field that got its name automatically apart from a field that simply has no name yet. There is also no simple flag on a field that tells me whether its name was chosen for me or chosen by me.

## What should happen

When my helper looks at each field, every field should already have its name filled in, whether I set it myself or it was chosen for me. Each field should also carry a clear flag that is true when the name was chosen automatically and false when I set it myself. That way my helper can make decisions based on that flag instead of guessing from an empty value.

## About this project

This project is a library that helps people write small classes that mostly hold data. Instead of writing lots of repetitive setup code by hand, a person describes the fields they want and the library writes the boring parts for them. It is used widely in Python programs to keep data-holding classes short and clear.

## Problem this solves

People who write helpers that adjust fields need to know which names were picked automatically, so they can replace or keep them without touching the names they chose themselves. Today they cannot tell the two apart, so they either overwrite names they wanted to keep or miss names they wanted to replace.

## What changed

Fields now arrive at a person's field helper with their automatic names already in place, instead of arriving empty. Each field also gains a flag that says whether its name was chosen automatically or set by hand. The old habit of checking for an empty name to detect an automatic one no longer matches how the fields arrive.

## Impact

Ease of use and correctness for people who write field helpers.

## User experience

Before: I write a helper that checks whether a field's name is empty to decide it was chosen automatically, but fields I named by hand and fields named for me both look the same in some cases, so my helper gets it wrong. After: I read the new flag on each field, and it plainly tells me whether the name was chosen for me, so my helper does the right thing every time.

- /workspace/docs/extending.md
- /workspace/tests/test_functional.py
- /workspace/tests/test_hooks.py
- /workspace/tests/test_make.py
- /workspace/tests/utils.py
